clue.text: Bring up opportunity to see Hitchcock movie

parts.note: to rear a child is to bring it up
a window is a limited stretch of time in which something can be done

explanation.surface: Someone raises the chance of an evening in front of an old thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring up' works twice over: it sounds like raising a subject and means raising a child. The film is Hitchcock's 1954 thriller, shot entirely from inside one apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: REAR WINDOW is the title of a Hitchcock picture, so the definition names the answer by category — one instance of his films.

clue.text: Does and bucks rampant in grass

indicators.note: in heraldry a beast rampant is rearing up on its hind legs, and anything rearing up in a down clue is read from the bottom of the light towards the top

parts.note: does are the females and bucks the males of one and the same animal

explanation.surface: Deer of both sexes charging about in long grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rampant' reads as wild behaviour and is really the heraldic pose, an animal up on its hind legs — which in a down light is an instruction to climb. A reed is a tall grass of wet ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A REED is a tall grass growing in marshes and riverbanks, so 'grass' is the plain category word for it.

clue.text: One (or 17) before Romeo

definitions.meaning: reads as a number or as a cross-reference to another entry in the grid; it is really a position in a list — first place, and also seventeen places back from R
Romeo is the NATO radio codeword for R, which is what fixes the list being counted along; the same two words also sit side by side on an Italian car badge

explanation.surface: A note pointing at other numbers in the puzzle and at somebody called Romeo.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is the giveaway: it is a NATO radio codeword, so the counting runs along that alphabet, where A stands first and R stands eighteenth — one place along, or seventeen places back. ALFA also fronts a famous car marque.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO alphabet ALFA is the codeword for A: the first entry, and seventeen places before Romeo, the codeword for R.

clue.text: Walnut? Not half! And a little Discovery or Fuji's cored, as prepared in diners, primarily

definitions.text: Walnut? Not half! And a little Discovery or Fuji's cored, as prepared in diners, primarily

indicators.note: only half of walnut is kept, its front three letters

parts.note: a little of the Discovery apple is just a taste of it, the opening letter D

indicators.note: coring an apple removes its middle, leaving only the outer letters of Fuji's

parts.note: the French a la, prepared in the style of, plus D, the first letter of diners as 'primarily' picks it

explanation.surface: A recipe note: walnuts, plenty of them, plus a cored Discovery or Fuji apple, as served in diners.
explanation.walkthrough: Discovery and Fuji are apple varieties, both cored for the dish. 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it halves walnut.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the classic dish of walnuts and chopped apple in mayonnaise, first made at a New York hotel.

clue.text: Greek character danced topless with subtlety

parts.note: nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: without its top the word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A Greek person dancing without a top on, delicately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' takes D off DANCED to leave ANCED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nuanced shows fine shades of meaning, which is exactly what subtlety is.

clue.text: A little yobbo near there, where you live

indicators.note: 'A little' asks for part of what follows rather than all of it, which is how a run of letters buried in the words gets flagged

parts.note: seven letters running straight on from the end of the first word, through the whole of the second, into the start of the third

explanation.surface: A minor thug hanging around near the place you call home.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are sitting in the open a few words before the definition, and long hidden phrases hide best exactly here — inside an ordinary noun phrase, where you read the words instead of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Where you live' is the planet, and ON EARTH is the phrase for being on it — the same words that sharpen a question like 'what on earth?'

clue.text: Revolutionary, loud apron-wearer

parts.note: Che Guevara is the crossword's standing revolutionary
f is forte, the musical direction for playing loud

explanation.surface: A loud-mouthed radical who happens to be wearing an apron.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are conventions worth banking: CHE is who a crossword means by a revolutionary, and F is the musician's forte, which turns up in dozens of clues a year.
explanation.definitionFit: A CHEF runs the professional kitchen, and the apron is that trade's uniform, so the definition names the answer by what it wears.

clue.text: Around end of dinner, hail her cab, mostly arranged in ranks

indicators.note: around in the sense of all over the place, so the gathered letters are scattered into a new order
end of picks the final letter

parts.note: last letter of dinner

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter of cab is dropped

explanation.surface: After a meal out, someone flags down a taxi for a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of dinner' gives R and 'cab, mostly' gives CA; with HAIL HER, mix the lot 'Around'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hierarchal is a variant of hierarchical: organised in graded levels, each tier above the next.

clue.text: Undergarment that goes on before blusher

definitions.meaning: the drapers' sense: the shaping garment worn beneath everything else, a corset or a girdle
the cosmetics sense: the base coat spread on the skin before any colour goes over it

explanation.surface: Getting dressed and made up, in the right order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undergarment' is placed first to keep you in the wardrobe, so the make-up sense arrives late — and the two meanings of FOUNDATION never touch except in a phrase about getting ready.
explanation.definitionFit: A foundation garment is shapewear worn underneath, and foundation is also the make-up base applied before blusher: one word, two dressing-table senses.

clue.text: Fixes ale to order and gets out of one's skin

indicators.note: putting something in order means moving things into new positions, and the letters take up new positions here

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, exactly the length being asked for

explanation.surface: A barman sorts the beer out to order while somebody leaps out of their skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets out of one's skin' borrows the idiom about jumping out of it in fright, and means the beauty-counter thing instead: scrubbing the dead outer layer away.
explanation.definitionFit: To EXFOLIATE is to take the dead surface layer off, so the answer really does get something out of one's skin.

clue.text: Fancy fellow's drop of bottled French water

indicators.note: a drop is the least amount of liquid you can take, so the word behind it parts with a single letter, its first

parts.note: the first letter of bottled
eau is French for water, as on a bottle of eau minérale

explanation.surface: A dandy with a little bottled French mineral water.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all drinks trolley, and 'drop' is the word doing the damage — a measure of liquid on one reading, an instruction about letters on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A BEAU is a woman's admirer or a showy dresser, so 'fancy fellow' catches both the courting sense and the peacock one.

clue.text: In turn, they'll get you going

definitions.meaning: reads as one after another, taking it in turns; what is meant is the turning itself, the twist of a wrist in a steering column
reads as encouragement from somebody keeping your spirits up; what is meant is starting a vehicle moving

explanation.surface: Colleagues taking it in turns to jolly you along and get you motivated.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separable wordplay to find: the whole clue is one definition with two readings. The plural is the hint, because a person who gets you going comes one at a time and IGNITION KEYS jangle in a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: IGNITION KEYS are what you turn to start an engine, so 'in turn' and 'get you going' both read literally once the human sense is dropped.

clue.text: Making racket — foregone conclusion — excellent: a huge piano!

parts.note: a racket is a swindle run as though it were a business, and a swindle is a con
a cert is British shorthand for a certainty — a dead cert
grand means splendid as well as large

explanation.surface: A string of exclamations: the noise, the inevitable outcome, and a magnificent instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' is the pivot. The surface wants the din a big piano makes; the wordplay wants the criminal sense, a protection racket. 'Cert' is worth learning in its own right — British for a sure thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A CONCERT GRAND is the largest grand piano made, the nine-foot instrument used on stage, so 'a huge piano' is plain description.

clue.text: Seconds, cheap in the extreme and most delicious

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for seconds on a stopwatch
crummy means cheap and shoddy, and in the extreme pushes it to its superlative

explanation.surface: Cut-price factory rejects turn out to taste wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' reads as the flawed goods on a market stall and gives up the stopwatch abbreviation instead. Scrummy is British nursery slang for delicious, a child's squashing of scrumptious.
explanation.definitionFit: SCRUMMIEST is the superlative of scrummy, so it means most delicious — the informal register, not the dictionary one.

clue.text: Department's leader reporting to top teacher, an idiot

indicators.note: a leader is the one out in front, so the word hands over the letter standing at its front

parts.note: the first letter of department
somebody who reports to you sits under you on the staff chart
the head is what a British school calls its principal

explanation.surface: A staffroom note: the department chief answers to the head, and someone is a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is built out of a school flow chart, which is what stops 'an idiot' at the end from looking like a definition — it reads as one more remark about the man.
explanation.definitionFit: A DUNDERHEAD is a blockhead, an old word for someone slow-witted, so 'an idiot' is a straight singular synonym.

clue.text: Acted like a steam train travelling over the moon

definitions.text: Acted like a steam train travelling
definitions.meaning: a locomotive puffing along makes the noise its own verb is named after, and the clue wants that verb in the past tense
the British idiom for delighted, the phrase footballers and lottery winners reach for

explanation.surface: A steam engine puffing along, thoroughly pleased with itself.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves define, so the sentence asserts nothing at all — and 'travelling over the moon' reads as one phrase, as though the engine were sailing past the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: CHUFFED is the past tense of chuff, the sound a steam engine makes, and it is also British slang for delighted, which is what 'over the moon' means.

clue.text: Hot air ignored? Do!

parts.note: h is the letter on a hot tap
the word is taken at face value, all three letters of it
to cut somebody is to snub them, to look straight past them in the street

explanation.surface: Empty boasting is brushed aside, with an order to get on with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is two letters long, which is what makes this hard: a do is a hairdo, and everything before it reads as a complete sentence about being snubbed.
explanation.definitionFit: A do is informal British for a hairdo — the styling itself — which is what a HAIRCUT gives you.

clue.text: Not fine, flaunted, displaying cards in deck like so

indicators.note: not fine means the fine letter is to be left out of the flaunted letters
displaying suggests putting letters out on show in a fresh layout, so they are reordered

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A card player shows off a hand while being anything but well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fine' takes F away from FLAUNTED, and 'displaying' rearranges the remaining LAUNTED. Cards still in the deck have not yet been handed out.
explanation.definitionFit: Cards remaining in the pack are those the dealer has not yet given out to the players.

clue.text: Some wrote her a note somewhere in Iran

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows and not the whole of it, which is the signal that a run of letters is sitting inside those words

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from the middle of the first word through to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Somebody left a short written message behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling with the extra E is the older transliteration, and it is what makes this work — the modern Tehran would not fit the letters these words offer. 'Some' is the only hint that anything is buried.
explanation.definitionFit: TEHERAN is Iran's capital, so 'somewhere in Iran' defines it by category: a place in the country rather than the country itself.

clue.text: Musical fashionable in the past

parts.note: chic is stylish, borrowed straight from the French
something in the past happened a while ago

explanation.surface: A show that used to be in vogue and no longer is.
explanation.walkthrough: One word carries the entire definition, and it defines by example — CHICAGO is a particular show rather than the category. The city it is named for never gets a mention.
explanation.definitionFit: CHICAGO is the Kander and Ebb stage musical, so the definition points at the answer through its genre — one instance of the form.

clue.text: Announced boxy workspace

indicators.note: 'Announced' means said out loud, so the clue is describing how the word sounds rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: a boxy thing is cubical, shaped like a cube — and said out loud that word is indistinguishable from the office one

explanation.surface: Somebody reads out a description of a square little office.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, one sound, different spellings: CUBICAL with an A is the cube-shaped adjective, CUBICLE with an E the partitioned desk. Only your ear connects them.
explanation.definitionFit: A CUBICLE is a partitioned-off desk space in an open-plan office, so 'workspace' is the plain noun for it.

clue.text: Musicians from China barmaid enlivened

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: a band is one thing made of many players, so the plural noun names what the answer is a collection of.

indicators.note: to enliven something is to stir it up, and letters stirred up do not stay in the order they were handed to you

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder, matching the enumeration exactly

explanation.surface: A barmaid from China brightens the whole pub up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From China' reads as a country of origin, and the players are Mexican — the words are in the clue only for their letters, which is what a long anagram counts on.
explanation.definitionFit: A MARIACHI BAND is the Mexican street ensemble of trumpets, violins and guitars, so 'musicians' is the plain category word.

clue.text: Foremost of peaks enveloping River Ucayali — here!

definitions.text: Foremost of peaks enveloping River Ucayali — here!

indicators.note: the leading letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Mountains rising around the Ucayali river in this country.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the Ucayali flows through the Andes of this South American country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ucayali is a major Amazon tributary that runs through the Andean country, ringed by high mountains.

clue.text: Remain conscious throughout Australia Day, finally

indicators.note: 'finally' asks for the letter each word finishes on, taken in the order the words arrive

parts.note: the last letter of conscious
the last letter of throughout
the last letter of Australia
the last letter of Day

explanation.surface: Keeping awake right through the national holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remain conscious' reads as one phrase and only the first word defines; everything after it is a queue of words giving up their final letters. Australia Day is the country's national holiday, 26 January.
explanation.definitionFit: To STAY somewhere is to remain there — the same verb in the same form, the everyday synonym.

clue.text: Your crossword compiler is only half there — always

indicators.note: 'only half there' says the name arrives at half length, so four of its eight letters are left behind

parts.note: the setter of this Observer puzzle signs himself with one eight-letter name

explanation.surface: The compiler confesses to being only half present, as he always is.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman writing his own name into a clue is a habit of this puzzle worth knowing, and 'only half there' is the joke twice: the letters are halved and the man is distracted.
explanation.definitionFit: EVER means at all times, so 'always' is a straight synonym — the sense in 'ever faithful', not the questioning 'did you ever?'

clue.text: Sporting fixture — racket bust — let rip

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters of racket are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: to vent is to let rip with one's feelings

explanation.surface: A tennis player's racket breaks and they unleash their anger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' looks like the tennis bat, but its letters are 'bust' into TRACKE. To vent anger is to let rip with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A track event is an athletics race run on the track, as opposed to a field event.

clue.text: Sea's movement even, you say?

indicators.note: 'you say' hands the clue to your ear: what counts is the noise the word makes, not the letters it is written with

parts.note: a match that finishes even is tied, and that word said out loud is what you write in the grid

explanation.surface: A remark that the sea's movement is level, pending confirmation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' is a word for level water as well as for a drawn match, so the surface talks about a calm sea while the mechanism wants the scoreboard sense. The two spellings share their letters and sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: The TIDE is the sea's twice-daily rise and fall, so 'sea's movement' names the answer by what it does.

clue.text: Stand-in actor to read European articles first

indicators.note: 'first' sends the piece it follows to the front of the answer instead of leaving it where the clue puts it

parts.note: the French indefinite article un and the German definite article der, laid end to end
to read a subject at university is to study it

explanation.surface: An actor is told to get through the European papers before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read' is the British university sense — you read history at Durham — and 'first' is what reorders the halves, since the articles are named after the verb and belong in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An UNDERSTUDY learns a part in order to go on when the lead cannot, which is exactly a stand-in actor.
